extra.message: FLASK_RUN_HOST=0.0.0.0 binds the Flask development server to all network interfaces. While expected in a container, combined with Flask dev server it exposes the debug interface to the network.

The Dockerfile uses the Flask development server (CMD ["flask", "run"]) which is single-threaded, has no production-grade security hardening, and when combined with DEBUG=True exposes the Werkzeug debugger.

Flash message content is rendered directly into the page. If the flash message contains user-controlled data or error details, it could expose sensitive information. While auto-escaped by default, category is not escaped.

The search_query variable (from request.args['search']) is rendered with the 'safe' filter, which disables Jinja2 auto-escaping. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript via the search parameter.

User input from the comment input field is directly appended to the DOM as HTML using jQuery's .append() method without any sanitization. An attacker can type malicious HTML/JS (e.g., ) which will execute in the browser.

The user's country field is rendered with the 'safe' filter, which disables auto-escaping. The country can be set during signup or profile update with no sanitization, allowing an attacker to store malicious JavaScript in their profile that executes when any user views the profile page.
The dummy data creation script uses MD5 for password hashing, creating database records with broken password hashes that match what the application produces.

The dummy data insertion script contains hardcoded plaintext passwords like 'super-secret', 'password123', 'my-secret', 'password', 'password1'. While this is seed data, these weak passwords, even when MD5-hashed, are trivially crackable.

The Flask application is configured without any Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection. Multiple forms (login, signup, upload, update_profile) and AJAX endpoints (delete file) accept POST requests using cookie-based session authentication without CSRF tokens. An attacker can forge requests on behalf of authenticated users.
The /api/v1/login endpoint has no rate limiting. An attacker can perform unlimited brute-force password guessing via the API.
The API login endpoint has no rate limiting or brute-force protection, allowing unlimited authentication attempts.
The API login endpoint uses the same weak MD5-based custom_hash function to verify passwords. All passwords stored in the database are MD5 hashes.
The JWT tokens are signed using the same weak hardcoded SECRET_KEY from config.py ('just_another_secret'). An attacker who discovers this key can forge valid JWT tokens for any user.
The JWT encoding uses algorithm='HS256' in the jwt.encode() call. While PyJWT 2.8.0 uses a strict algorithm check, the algorithm string format could potentially cause confusion.

The @token_required decorator is commented out (line 152), making the UserProfile.get() endpoint accessible without any authentication. Any unauthenticated attacker can retrieve any user's profile information by providing a user_id query parameter.

The @token_required decorator is commented out on the UserProfile resource's get() method. Any unauthenticated user can query any user's profile by providing any user_id, exposing sensitive fields like role, permissions, email, and team.

The @token_required decorator on the UserProfile.get endpoint is commented out, leaving it completely unauthenticated. Any unauthenticated attacker can retrieve any user's profile information (username, email, country, role, permissions, team) by supplying a user_id parameter.

The UserProfile endpoint not only lacks authentication but also exposes sensitive fields: username, email, country, role, permissions, and team. An unauthenticated attacker can enumerate all users and extract their roles/permissions for targeted attacks.

The UserProfile GET endpoint has the @token_required decorator commented out. Any unauthenticated user can query any user's profile by providing a user_id query parameter, exposing sensitive profile information.

The UserProfile endpoint retrieves user profile data by a user-supplied user_id query parameter without scoping to the authenticated user. Even if authentication were enabled, any authenticated user could read any other user's profile.
The /api/v1/update-profile endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to submit unlimited profile update requests, potentially causing database load or data integrity issues.
The print(session) statement in the API update-profile handler logs the entire session dictionary to stdout, potentially exposing session data in server logs.
The @token_required decorator is commented out (lines 221-222), making the UserDelete endpoint accessible without any authentication. Any unauthenticated attacker can delete any user account by ID.
The @token_required decorator is commented out on the UserDelete resource's delete() method. Any unauthenticated user can delete any user account by providing a user_id.

The UserDelete endpoint has the @token_required decorator commented out (line 220-221), making it accessible to unauthenticated users. Anyone can call this endpoint to delete any user by providing their user_id. The openapi docstring even explicitly notes this as a 'Broken Function Level Authorization vulnerability'.
The UserDelete endpoint deletes a user by user_id from the URL path with no ownership or authorization check. Any authenticated user can delete any other user's account.
The ProfilePicture resource's post() method has no authentication check at all. Any unauthenticated attacker can update any user's profile picture by providing the username and a URL.
The /api/v1/update_picture endpoint has no rate limiting. An attacker can trigger unlimited HTTP requests to arbitrary URLs (SSRF) without any request frequency controls.

The requests.get() call in the profile picture update endpoint has no timeout configured. An attacker can provide a URL that hangs indefinitely, blocking the server thread and causing denial of service.

The update_picture endpoint fetches a user-provided URL using requests.get() without any validation or restriction on the URL scheme or target. An attacker can make the server send requests to internal services (localhost, internal network, cloud metadata endpoints).

The session cookie configuration does not set SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE, which defaults to False in Flask. This means the session cookie is transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, allowing network-level attackers to intercept it via man-in-the-middle attacks.
The DEBUG flag is set to True in the application configuration. Flask debug mode exposes an interactive debugger and allows arbitrary code execution through the Werkzeug debugger console.

The SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY is set to False, meaning JavaScript in the browser can access the session cookie via document.cookie. This nullifies one of the primary defenses against XSS-based session theft.
The Flask SECRET_KEY and JWT signing key is hardcoded as 'just_another_secret' in source code. This weak, hardcoded secret can be used to forge session cookies and JWT tokens.

The Flask SECRET_KEY is set to 'just_another_secret', which is a weak, guessable string. Flask uses this key to sign session cookies, CSRF tokens, and flash messages. An attacker who knows or guesses this key can forge arbitrary session cookies.

The filename parameter in the delete route is used directly with os.path.join and os.remove without sanitization. Although a DB ownership check exists, if a file with a path traversal name exists in the database, it could be deleted outside the intended directory.
The login route has no rate limiting or brute-force protection. An attacker can make unlimited POST requests to /login to enumerate valid usernames and brute-force passwords.
Passwords are stored as MD5 hashes but compared using an equality check against computed hash. While not plaintext comparison, the MD5 hash is weak and the comparison leaks timing information.
The login handler uses the custom_hash() function (MD5) to compare passwords against stored hashes, perpetuating the use of broken cryptography for authentication.

After successful authentication, the session ID is not regenerated using session.regenerate(). An attacker who tricks a victim into using a known session ID before login can hijack the victim's session after authentication.
The /signup endpoint has no rate limiting. An attacker can create thousands of fake accounts to exhaust server resources, fill the database, or perform spam campaigns.
The signup handler uses the custom_hash() function (MD5) to hash new user passwords before storing them in the database.
With DEBUG=True, the Flask debugger and detailed error pages reveal internal information including stack traces, source code snippets, and file paths when errors occur.
After user registration, session variables are set on the existing session without regeneration. The same session fixation attack vector applies as with the login handler.

The search_query parameter from request.args is directly interpolated into a SQL query using an f-string. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary SQL commands by providing a malicious search parameter.

The get_user_details_from_database function returns all columns from the users table (SELECT *), including the password hash. This full user object is passed to the profile template context, exposing the password hash even if not rendered.

The application uses cookie-based session authentication but has no CSRF protection on any state-changing routes (POST to /update_profile, /upload, /delete/<filename>). An attacker can craft a malicious page that submits requests on behalf of an authenticated victim.

The update_profile handler accepts role and permissions fields from the request form if present, without any authorization check. A regular user can escalate privileges to admin by sending 'role=admin' in their profile update request, even though these fields are hidden in the UI.

The update_profile handler accepts role and permissions fields from the HTTP request form data. Although these fields are commented out in the HTML template, any user can submit a POST request with 'role=admin&permissions=all' to escalate their privileges to administrator.

The update_profile function unconditionally accepts 'role' and 'permissions' fields from the request form data without any server-side authorization check. Although the HTML template has these fields commented out, an attacker can craft a POST request with role=admin and permissions=all to escalate their privileges to administrator.

The update_profile handler reads 'role' and 'permissions' fields directly from the request form data and uses them to update the user record in the database. Although the template has these fields commented out, an attacker can send them in a crafted POST request to escalate privileges.
The update_profile endpoint reads the 'permissions' field directly from the HTTP request form and updates the user's permissions. Any authenticated user can grant themselves elevated permissions.

After updating a profile, the user is redirected to url_for('profile'). When the username changes, the session is updated, but there's no open redirect here since url_for generates a path, not a full URL.

File upload has no validation on file type, content, or size. An attacker can upload executable files (.py, .sh, .php), HTML files with JavaScript, or extremely large files to cause denial of service.

The uploaded file's filename is used directly in os.path.join() and file.save() without sanitization. An attacker can use a filename like '../../etc/cronjob' to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem.

The filename parameter from the URL path is passed directly to send_from_directory without sanitization. An attacker who can guess or enumerate filenames can read arbitrary files outside the upload directory using '../' sequences.
The /uploads/profile_pictures/<filename> route serves profile pictures with no authentication check. Any unauthenticated user can access any user's profile picture.
The profile_pictures route has no authentication or authorization check. Any user (or unauthenticated visitor) can access any user's profile picture by guessing or enumerating filenames.

The profile_pictures route has no authentication or authorization check, allowing any user to access profile pictures by guessing numeric filenames (e.g., 1.png, 2.png). While the file path itself is simple, there's no ownership verification.

The filename parameter from the URL is used in os.path.join() to construct a file path for deletion. An attacker can provide a filename with '../' sequences to delete arbitrary files outside the upload directory.

The custom_hash function uses MD5 for password hashing, which is cryptographically broken and can be reversed with trivial computational effort. This function is used in both login (line 50) and signup (line 93) flows.
The custom_hash function uses MD5 for password hashing, which is cryptographically broken and can be reversed instantly using rainbow tables. All user passwords are hashed with MD5.

The session cookie is configured but only sets SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY (to False) and SESSION_COOKIE_NAME. The SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE flag is not set, meaning the cookie will be sent over unencrypted HTTP connections.
